speaker: Karri Saarinen
title: Inside Linear: Building with taste, craft, and focus | Karri Saarinen
question: When launching an early-stage B2B software product, why does onboarding users in small, selective cohorts work better than opening access to everyone at once?
guest: We were very selective because we knew we didn't support everything early on, and we wanted to stay focused on building a version that worked well for a specific set of companies rather than trying to address everyone in the world in the first months. In the beginning, I read the waitlist surveys in a spreadsheet, emailed invite links manually, and followed up a few days later to ask what people thought. We invited maybe ten people a week at first. The reason we did it that way is that if you invite everyone or too many people at once to very early-stage software, all of them will hit the same bugs and the same problems, and they'll all send you the same feedback, which feels like wasted effort. Instead, we ran cohorts: we'd invite one batch, hear what was broken or missing, fix it, and only then invite the next cohort to surface the next set of issues. That was a much more effective way to do initial development than letting everyone in right at the beginning.

points.core: Opening broadly causes every early user to hit the exact same bugs simultaneously.
points.note: Accept: mass early onboarding floods the team with redundant reports of identical defects, wasting effort. Do not credit: generic concerns about server scaling or customer support volume.

points.core: Sequential cohorts let teams fix blockers between waves so each batch surfaces new issues.
points.note: Accept: inviting a small batch, fixing what breaks, then inviting the next batch maximizes unique feedback per user. Do not credit: vague advice to 'gather feedback iteratively'.

points.core: Filtering early signups by existing stack lets teams ship for one supported environment first.
points.note: Accept: selecting waitlist users who match current integrations or company size avoids trying to support every edge case upfront. Do not credit: generic advice to 'find early adopters' without the compatibility/scope-narrowing mechanism.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Small, selective cohorts work better because an early-stage product's scarcest resource is learning, not reach. With a handful of carefully chosen customers, the team can onboard each one by hand, watch where they get stuck, and talk to them directly. That produces rich, interpretable feedback instead of a flood of noisy signals from users who were never a good fit.

Selectivity also lets you pick customers who match your ideal profile and feel the problem acutely, so their feedback steers the product toward the right market rather than pulling it in conflicting directions.

Cohorts also create a clean iteration loop: you fix what the first group struggled with, then test whether the next group activates and retains better. Opening to everyone blurs that comparison.

Finally, it limits risk. B2B buyers have low tolerance for bugs, weak support, and missing features, and a bad first impression is hard to reverse in a market with a finite number of accounts and strong word of mouth. A gated rollout keeps support load manageable, turns early users into successful reference customers, and saves the broad launch for when the product and onboarding can actually convert the attention.

points.why: The response attributes noisy feedback to poor-fit users and omits the duplication that occurs when many users encounter the same bugs.
The response describes fixing problems between cohorts to measure activation and retention gains, but it does not explain how those fixes let later cohorts surface new issues.
The response selects for market fit and urgency without tying selection to supported integrations, company size, or other constraints that narrow what the team must build.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Onboarding early-stage B2B users in small, selective cohorts protects both product direction and market reputation while accelerating learning. Because B2B software must fit into existing team workflows, permissions, and integrations, early friction quickly stalls adoption. Handpicking cohorts that match a focused ideal customer profile—companies acutely feeling the core problem—ensures feedback carries high signal rather than pulling the roadmap toward noisy requests from poor-fit users. Small batches also let founders provide white-glove onboarding, observe real usage firsthand, and fix critical gaps between waves so each new cohort experiences a meaningfully stronger product without overwhelming engineering or support.

Just as importantly, B2B markets have finite buyer pools and high trust barriers. Opening access broadly to an unpolished product risks burning scarce prospects who rarely give a startup a second look, whereas curating a small group of successful early adopters turns them into design partners, case studies, and reference customers that make broader sales far easier.

points.why: The response cites engineering and support load without explaining that broad access generates duplicate reports of the same bugs.
The response says fixes between waves improve the product for the next cohort but does not explain that those fixes let later cohorts surface new issues.
The response selects users by how acutely they feel the problem without tying selection to environments the product already supports.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Small, selective cohorts work better because an early B2B product is still unfinished, and the team can only give close attention to a limited number of customers at once. With a handful of well-chosen accounts, founders can personally onboard each one, watch where people get stuck, and fix problems before the next group arrives. Each cohort then starts with a better product than the one before it.

Choosing who gets in also improves what you learn. If you pick customers who match your ideal profile and feel the problem sharply, their feedback shows whether you have real product-market fit. Opening access to everyone brings in mixed use cases and pulls the roadmap in many directions.

Cohorts also limit the damage when things go wrong. Bugs, missing integrations or security gaps affect a few forgiving design partners rather than many prospects who might churn and complain publicly. In B2B, where buyers ask each other for references, that matters.

Finally, controlled access gives you clean data on activation and retention for each cohort, and limited spots create a sense of exclusivity that strengthens commitment and turns early users into references and case studies.

points.why: The response says broad access exposes more prospects to bugs but never explains that those users would report the same defects and duplicate feedback.
The response commits to fixing blockers before admitting the next cohort, so the next group can uncover issues beyond those already fixed.
quotes: watch where people get stuck, and fix problems before the next group arrives.
Each cohort then starts with a better product than the one before it.

points.why: The response selects for ideal-customer fit and urgency without connecting eligibility to the integrations or operating environments the product already supports.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Onboarding early-stage B2B users in small, selective cohorts protects both product quality and learning speed. Because B2B software typically embeds into complex team workflows, early versions inevitably have rough edges, missing integrations, and unclear setup paths. Opening access to everyone at once floods a small team with support requests and conflicting feedback from poor-fit users, making it difficult to separate genuine product gaps from noise.

Selective cohorts let you hand-pick customers who closely match your ideal profile and feel the problem acutely enough to tolerate early friction. With a manageable group, founders can deliver high-touch onboarding, watch how teams actually use the product, and fix core bugs or workflow bottlenecks before inviting the next wave. Each cohort also acts as a clean experiment, letting you verify that retention and time-to-value improve with every iteration. Finally, pacing access preserves your reputation—preventing premature churn and negative word-of-mouth—while turning satisfied early adopters into credible references before a broader launch.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Small, selective cohorts let you learn why customers adopt the product, where they get stuck, and what makes them come back. Start with companies that have the problem you’re solving and can try the product in a real workflow. With only a few accounts at a time, you can watch users get started, talk to the people who stall, and tell whether the problem is setup friction, a missing capability, or a weak fit.

Each cohort gives you a chance to fix what you observed and see whether the next group reaches value faster and needs less hands-on support. Opening access to everyone at once can overwhelm a small team and burn first impressions with customers who might have stuck around after those fixes. Once similar accounts can get started and keep using the product with less help, you have a stronger basis for expanding access.

The response selects companies by problem fit and ability to try a real workflow without tying selection to an environment the product already supports.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Small, selective cohorts let an early team learn faster from each customer. When the first customers share a problem the product aims to solve, the team can watch them use it in a real workflow and see where they get stuck. If several customers stall at the same integration, the team can fix it and see whether the next cohort gets through without help.

A broad launch mixes customers with different needs and can generate more support requests than the team can handle. Promising customers may leave before they see value, and the team may never learn why. Cohorts keep that risk manageable while revealing which customers benefit most and what it takes to get them up and running. Once customers consistently reach that point with less hands-on help, the team has a sounder basis for expanding access.

points.why: The response links broad access to higher support volume without explaining how simultaneous exposure to the same defects generates redundant reports.
The response describes using the next cohort to verify an integration fix but does not explain how clearing blockers between waves lets later cohorts surface new issues.
The response groups users by a shared problem without tying selection to compatibility with what the product already supports.
